t: For some 14,000 years the people of the Japanese archipelago lived mainly by hunting, gathering and fishing, yet many settled in villages, reaching a considerable degree of sedentism and cultural complexity.
Jōmon potters made the world’s oldest known ceramics, around 14,500 BCE; their pottery was typically decorated by pressing cords into the wet clay, the pattern that gives the culture its name.
The Jōmon people later mixed with the Yayoi rice farmers: modern Japanese carry part of their ancestry, and two Jōmon populations of Hokkaido merged to form the proto-Ainu.
dyk: A domesticated peach, already similar to modern cultivated forms, appears at Jōmon sites around 4700–4400 BCE, earlier than a variety so close to modern peaches is attested in China itself.
ev: Jōmon hunter-gatherers make the world’s oldest known pottery, fragments of which survive at Odai Yamamoto I
As the glaciers melt at the end of the last glacial period, rising seas separate the archipelago from the Asian mainland
The Early Jōmon begins in the warm Holocene climatic optimum, with a rise in population and larger villages
A domesticated peach, apparently brought from China, appears at Jōmon sites
The Middle Jōmon, the warmest phase, produces “flame style” vessels, dogū figurines and more elaborate pit-houses
The climate cools and the population appears to contract dramatically
Korean-type settlements bringing wet rice farming and bronze and iron metallurgy are established in western Kyushu
Edward S. Morse finds cord-marked sherds and gives the culture its name

f.homeland: The Japanese archipelago from Hokkaido to Kyushu, with most people in Honshu and Kyushu; the Jōmon were mostly absent from Okinawa and the Ryukyu Islands. Key sites: Odai Yamamoto I, Kamikuroiwa, the Fukui cave and the Ikawazu shell mound at Tahara.
f.period: c. 14,000–300 BCE: Incipient 13,750–8,500 BCE, Initial 8,500–5,000, Early 5,000–3,520, Middle 3,520–2,470, Late 2,470–1,250 and Final 1,250–500 BCE, the end of the Final phase now refined to c. 300 BCE.
f.known: cord-marked pottery among the oldest in the world; “flame style” vessels; dogū figurines; lacquerware; magatama curved stone beads; pit-houses; shell middens; tended groves of chestnut and lacquer trees; the early domestication of the adzuki bean
f.sources: Excavated sites and shell middens; pottery typology (some 70 styles) and radiocarbon dating; skeletal and dental studies; ancient DNA and full-genome analyses; loanwords in Japanese. The Jōmon left no writing.
